title: A practical guide to Small Area Estimation for Urban Analytics
text:
Small area estimation for Urban Analytics

Urban researchers often want to use survey data at the scale where urban questions are asked: neighbourhoods, census blocks, transport zones, or other local units. This may involve comparing places, monitoring change over time, identifying local inequalities, or linking survey outcomes to area-level conditions. The problem is that most surveys are not designed to support reliable estimates at all geographic levels and time periods. When responses are broken down by area and year, some cells have only a few respondents and others have none.
This tutorial presents a workflow for choosing spatio-temporal Bayesian small-area estimation (SAE) methods for urban analytics. It focuses on method choice and shows how these approaches can be implemented in INLA.



Bayesian inference and INLA

Bayesian inference is used to combine survey evidence, auxiliary predictors, neighbouring-area structure, year-to-year structure, and uncertainty from sparse cells in one estimation framework. One advantage is that uncertainty of a modelled estimate is returned as posterior distributions for each estimate, which faciliates interpretation in policy contexts.
For code implementation, the examples are fitted with R-INLA, the R interface to Integrated Nested Laplace Approximation. INLA provides deterministic approximate Bayesian inference for latent Gaussian models, usually much faster than MCMC for this workflow.



Tutorial structure

The tutorial is selective. It covers the SAE methods most relevant to common Urban Analytics survey and auxiliary datasets, with the choice driven by outcome type, available survey information, auxiliary data, and population structure.


Estimation setup
Start by specifying the estimand: outcome, target population, areas, and time periods. This defines the area-time cells that need estimates and the inputs required for each possible route.
Direct estimation
Compute survey design-based estimates and sampling variances for observed area-time cells. If these estimates are precise enough and have adequate coverage, direct estimation may be sufficient.
Fay–Herriot area-level model
Use this route when direct estimates exist but are too noisy or incomplete, and the available auxiliary data are area-level predictors. The model smooths direct estimates across predictors, neighbouring areas, and time periods.
Battese–Harter–Fuller unit-level model Use this route when survey microdata are available and the outcome can be modelled at respondent or household level. The fitted unit-level relationship is then aggregated to area-time estimates using area-level summaries of the predictors.
Multilevel Regression with Poststratification (MRP)
Use this route when population counts are available for poststratification cells, such as area by age by sex. The model predicts outcomes for each population cell and weights those predictions back to area-time estimates.




Tutorial data

The tutorial uses synthetic datasets based on the National Survey for Wales.
The maps and estimates illustrate the workflow and should not be interpreted as empirical findings for specific places in Wales. The synthetic dataset construction and preprocessing steps are described in the estimation setup step.



About the project

The tutorial is part of the TRACK-UK project by the City Modelling Lab.
TRACK-UK develops spatial and statistical methods for analysing mobility patterns at fine geographic scales and assessing their implications for transport decarbonisation in the UK. The project works with academic, policy, and industry partners to produce evidence for transport and energy policy.
For questions about the tutorial, contact:

Anna Freni-Sterrantino - The Alan Turing Institute
Esra Suel - University College London; University of Zurich

title: SAE Toolkit
text: This SAE toolkit shows how to adapt the tutorial workflow to your own survey, geography, and outcome by mapping your data to a common schema and applying reusable scripts.

This data preparation step introduces the survey source, defines the estimand, documents the synthetic geography, and explains the analysis-ready datasets used by the estimation workflows that follow.

title: Setting up for the estimation workflow
text:
1 The Survey Microdata
The tutorial uses a synthetic teaching dataset based on the three survey waves of the National Survey for Wales (NSW) in 2020-2021, 2022-2023, and 2024-2025.
The NSW is a repeated cross-sectional survey of people in Wales, with annual survey periods covering topics such as transport, health, education, public services, housing, internet access, climate change, and the Welsh language. The cleaned microdata combine three survey periods into one harmonised survey microdata.
Since the survey responses are originally geo-indexed at the Local Authority level, but the practical tutorial estimates indicators at MSOA level, we use a synthetic MSOA assignment. The cleaned survey file keeps each respondent’s Local Authority and assigns a synthetic MSOA within that Local Authority using deterministic random allocation. As such, estimates produced from these data should not be read as substantive findings about individual MSOAs in Wales.
This design has two purposes:

Higher spatial resolution for tutorial purposes. Possible to demonstrate MSOA-level direct estimation, area-level SAE, spatial modelling, and MRP-style poststratification.
Privacy and disclosure protection. The assigned MSOA is not the respondent’s true MSOA, so we avoid presenting fine-grained respondent locations.







Note



From here on, the survey period labels are simplified to their end year. For example, the 2020-2021 survey wave is labelled as and referred to as the 2021 wave.

title: Setting up for the estimation workflow
text:
2 Data Preparation Pipeline



Preparation pipeline for analysis-ready inputs



2.1 Defining The Estimand
The estimand is the quantity we want to estimate. It should be defined before preparing the survey indicator or choosing a model, because it determines the outcome coding, denominator, target geography, time period, auxiliary predictors, and poststratification requirements.

Estimate what outcome among which population, across which geography and time period.

In spatio-temporal SAE, this estimand is evaluated for every combination of area and time period. Each combination is an area-time cell: one observation we want to estimate. In this worked example, one area-time cell is one MSOA in one survey wave year, or an MSOA-year cell.
In this tutorial, the estimand is:






Target estimand





Outcome and Population: Share of Adults who walk for transport daily
Geography: MSOAs in Wales
Time: 2021, 2023, and 2025






2.2 Preparing The Survey Indicator
Since we are interested in whether our respondents walk frequently as the main mode of transport, we can code the indicator from AtFrqWlk10, the active-travel frequency question for walking.



Field
Definition




Indicator name
freq_walker


Raw survey variable
AtFrqWlk10


Positive case
AtFrqWlk10 == 1, walking daily


Negative case
Walking but not daily


Missing
Missing, invalid, or not asked



Since the survey question was administered to all respondents during some survey periods and subsampled in others, the corresponding weight variable selection rule is as follows:

Use SampleTravelWeight in survey waves where this question was asked to a subsample and the corresponding weight for this module exists,
Use SampleAdultWeight in survey waves where this question was asked to the main sample.

The walking survey indicator input has one row per respondent-wave:



Column
Meaning




unit_id
Unique respondent identifier


time_id
Survey year


area_id
Synthetic MSOA assignment


strata
Local Authority stratum


indicator
Binary response (i.e., freq_walker)


weight
Matched weight

2.3 Preparing Auxiliary Data

2.3.1 Unit-Level Predictors
Unit-level SAE models need respondent predictors that can be used to model the target outcome. For this example, to model individual freq_walker, we extract or transform these unit-level predictors from the survey microdata for each individual respondent row:







Column
Meaning




age
Respondent age


sex
Respondent sex (1 for Male, 2 for Female)


car_access
Binary household car access predictor (1 for car/van available, 0 for none available)





2.3.2 Area Predictors and Area Summaries
SAE models sometimes call for area-level predictors that plausibly explain spatial differences in daily walking. The six area predictors are drawn from Census 2021 bulk tables at MSOA level. These variables are chosen because daily walking is likely to vary with population composition, density, car access, and local work or study patterns.








Group
Variables
Why include




Demographic
Female share; mean adult age
Capture broad differences in population composition


Core
Population density; share of households with at least one car or van
Capture urban form and car access


Additional
Share working from home; share full-time students
Capture wider work- and study-pattern differences related to travel behaviour



The area-predictor input has one row per MSOA:



Column
Meaning




area_id
MSOA estimation area


msoa_name
MSOA name


raw_*
Raw predictors


scaled_*
Z-scored versions for model input





2.3.3 Poststratification Table
A population poststratification table is needed to apply the fitted estimation model to the target population. We use a three-variable poststratification table with age_band, sex, and car_access, sourced from ONS UK Census 2021. Because this detailed table is only observed for 2021, the 2021 age-sex-car composition is reused for the 2023 and 2025 estimands.
The richer poststratification output has one row per area-time-age-sex-car-access combination:



Column
Meaning




area_id
MSOA estimation area


time_id
Survey year


age_band
Census age band


sex
Sex category (1 for Male, 2 for Female)


car_access
Household car-access category


pop_count
Population count









Note



We also demonstrate a shallower poststratification setup where counts are available for more years but only by age and sex. An example is the ONS MSOA quinary age-by-sex population estimates.

title: Unit-Level SAE Modelling (Battese–Harter–Fuller)
text:
Theory in brief



The unit-level route models respondent outcomes directly. For the area-time target \mu_{jt}, a simple mixed-model form is:

Y_{ijt} = \alpha + x_{ijt}^{T}\beta + u_j + v_t + \epsilon_{ijt},

where x_{ijt} contains unit-level predictors, u_j is an area effect, and v_t is a time effect. The area effect can be replaced by a structured spatial effect, and a temporal effect v_t can be added to represent wave-to-wave dependence. To estimate the target for an area-time cell, the fitted model is evaluated using the corresponding population-level auxiliary summaries \bar{x}_{jt}:

\hat{\mu}_{jt}^{\mathrm{BHF}}
=
\widehat{\mathbb{E}}(Y \mid j,t,\bar{x}_{jt}).
Code
library(dplyr)
library(readr)
library(stringr)
library(tidyr)
library(sf)
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)
library(spdep)
library(INLA)
library(tibble)
library(purrr)
library(scales)

base_path <- here::here("data")
domain_frame <- read_csv(file.path(base_path, "clean", "domain_msoayear.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
share_label <- label_percent(accuracy = 0.1)
pp_label <- label_number(accuracy = 0.1, scale = 100, suffix = " pp")

msoa_boundaries <- st_read(
  file.path(base_path, "boundaries-msoa.geojson"),
  quiet = TRUE
) |>
  rename(area_id = all_of("MSOA21CD")) |>
  filter(str_starts(area_id, "W"))

title: Unit-Level SAE Modelling (Battese–Harter–Fuller)
text:
Estimation approach






Target estimand





Outcome and Population: Share of Adults who walk for transport daily
Geography: MSOAs in Wales
Time: 2021, 2023, and 2025




Unit-level SAE models respondent records directly instead of modelling pre-aggregated direct estimates. For our estimand, the Battese–Harter–Fuller model estimates the binary frequent-walking indicator from survey records using unit-level age, sex, and car_access predictors, together with spatial and temporal random effects.
The fitted model is then used to predict the target MSOA-year estimates using MSOA-level summaries of age, sex, and car access, obtained from ONS UK Census 2021. This avoids relying directly on unstable area-level direct estimates, but introduces new assumptions about how adequately or inadequately area-level summaries represent the population composition.

title: Unit-Level SAE Modelling (Battese–Harter–Fuller)
text:
1 Prepare model and aggregation data
Before preparing the model inputs, we create consistent numeric indices for each area and survey year so that INLA can attach random effects to the correct area and period, as well as a Queen-contiguity adjacency graph .adj as input, similar to what we did in the previous FH model estimation.

area_levels <- sort(unique(domain_frame[["area_id"]]))
time_levels <- sort(unique(domain_frame[["time_id"]]))

area_index <- tibble(
  area_id = area_levels,
  area_inla_id = seq_along(area_levels)
)

time_index <- tibble(
  time_id = time_levels,
  time_inla_id = seq_along(time_levels)
)


msoa_boundaries_sorted <- msoa_boundaries |>
  inner_join(area_index, by = "area_id") |>
  arrange(area_inla_id)

msoa_neighbours <- poly2nb(
  msoa_boundaries_sorted,
  queen = TRUE,
  row.names = msoa_boundaries_sorted$area_id
)

spatial_graph_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".adj")

nb2INLA(
  file = spatial_graph_file,
  nb = msoa_neighbours
)

We now prepare the two datasets needed for the unit-level INLA workflow:

model_data contains the sampled respondent records used to fit the model.
aggregation_data contains one row for each area-time cell we want to estimate.


1.1 Respondent model data
The respondent model data has one row per sampled person. For this example we use:

indicator as the binary response, our target;
age as a unit-level predictor;
female as a binary unit-level predictor;
car_access as a unit-level predictor;
time_id as the survey wave year identifier;
area_id as the area identifier;



Code
walking_indicator <- read_csv(file.path(base_path, "clean", "surveyind_freqwalk.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  select(unit_id, time_id, area_id, indicator, age, sex, car_access) |>
  mutate(female = as.integer(sex == 2))

model_data <- walking_indicator |>
  left_join(area_index, by = "area_id") |>
  left_join(time_index, by = "time_id") |>
  drop_na(indicator, area_id, time_id, age, female, car_access) |>
  select(
    unit_id,
    area_id,
    time_id,
    indicator,
    age,
    female,
    car_access,
    time_inla_id,
    area_inla_id
  ) |>
  arrange(time_id, area_inla_id)

title: Unit-Level SAE Modelling (Battese–Harter–Fuller)
text:
2 Fit and evaluate models
We fit linear mixed models to respondent-level records, then use them to predict area-time means. Because the response variable is binary, the fitted values are interpreted as predicted probabilities.
We specify three unit-level models to evaluate at the next step:








Model
Name
Specifications




M1
+TempSpatial
Respondent outcome with a temporal random walk and BYM2 spatial MSOA effect


M2
+Demographic
M1 plus respondent age and sex


M3
+CarAccess
M2 plus respondent-level car access




m1_formula <- indicator ~
  1 +
  f(time_inla_id, model = "rw1", constr = TRUE) +
  f(
    area_inla_id,
    model = "bym2",
    graph = spatial_graph_file,
    scale.model = TRUE,
    constr = TRUE
  )

m2_formula <- indicator ~
  age +
  female +
  f(time_inla_id, model = "rw1", constr = TRUE) +
  f(
    area_inla_id,
    model = "bym2",
    graph = spatial_graph_file,
    scale.model = TRUE,
    constr = TRUE
  )

m3_formula <- indicator ~
  age +
  female +
  car_access +
  f(time_inla_id, model = "rw1", constr = TRUE) +
  f(
    area_inla_id,
    model = "bym2",
    graph = spatial_graph_file,
    scale.model = TRUE,
    constr = TRUE
  )

model_formulas <- list(
  "M1 +TempSpatial" = m1_formula,
  "M2 +Demographic" = m2_formula,
  "M3 +CarAccess" = m3_formula
)

Conceptually, the workflow has two steps: fit the respondent-level model, then evaluate it for each area-time. We implement this by binding the observed respondent rows and the area-time aggregation rows into a single input table before fitting. The area-time rows to have their estimates predicted have indicator = NA, signalling to INLA to return fitted values for them.

model_agg_data <- bind_rows(
  model_data |>
    mutate(row_type = "model"),
  aggregation_data |>
    mutate(
      row_type = "aggregation",
      indicator = NA_real_
    )
) |>
  select(
    row_type, 
    indicator, 
    age, 
    female, 
    car_access, 
    time_inla_id, 
    area_inla_id
    )

fit_bhf_model <- function(formula) {
  inla(
    formula = formula,
    family = "gaussian",
    data = model_agg_data,
    control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE),
    control.compute = list(waic = TRUE, config = TRUE)
  )
}

bhf_fits <- lapply(model_formulas, fit_bhf_model)







Note



When fitting unit-level BHF models with INLA, these arguments are needed:

control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE) ensures that fitted values are returned for the full input table, so the predictions for the aggregation rows can be extracted after fitting.
control.compute = list(waic = TRUE) requests WAIC for comparing model fit across candidate specifications.



To compare the fitted models’ overall performance, we again use WAIC as a first check, a global predictive-fit measure returned by INLA. Lower values indicate better expected prediction after penalising model complexity. Here, the lower WAIC for M3 shows that adding the car-access predictor improves the model predictive power as expected.


Code
model_waic <- imap_dfr(
  bhf_fits,
  \(fit, model_name) {
    tibble(
      model = model_name,
      waic = fit$waic$waic,
      eff_params = fit$waic$p.eff
    )
  }
) |>
  arrange(waic)

title: Unit-Level SAE Modelling (Battese–Harter–Fuller)
text:
3 Final estimates and uncertainty
Using M3 as the selected model, we extract predictions for the target area-time rows, marked in the INLA input as row_type == "aggregation". We then report the posterior mean as the final estimate and use the lower and upper bounds of the 95% credible interval to describe uncertainty.
In practice, modelled estimates should always be reported alongside the direct-estimate metadata. This keeps the sample size, direct estimate, and direct-estimate variance in the final output, making it easier to compare the modelled result with the survey evidence it builds on.

bhf_m3_fitted_values <- bhf_fits[["M3 +CarAccess"]]$summary.fitted.values |>
  as_tibble() |>
  slice(which(model_agg_data$row_type == "aggregation"))

bhf_m3_results <- bind_cols(
  aggregation_data |> select(area_id, msoa_name, time_id),
  bhf_m3_fitted_values
) |>
  transmute(
    area_id,
    msoa_name,
    time_id,
    bhf_estimate = pmin(pmax(mean, 0), 1),
    bhf_variance = sd^2,
    bhf_lower = pmin(pmax(.data[["0.025quant"]], 0), 1), # clipped to [0,1] since estimate is a share
    bhf_upper = pmin(pmax(.data[["0.975quant"]], 0), 1), # clipped to [0,1] since estimate is a share
    bhf_ci_width = bhf_upper - bhf_lower
  )

Compared with the mapped direct estimates, the modelled estimates show a more plausible spatial pattern: more urban areas in south Wales have higher rates of daily walking among adults, while the sporadic jaggedness seen in low-sample regions is smoothed. The scatterplot below shows that the BHF estimates are in fact much smoother than the direct estimates and closer to the Fay–Herriot estimates, as expected from a model-based approach that borrows strength across area-time cells.


Code
fh_final_estimates <- read_csv(file.path(base_path, "freqwalk_estimates_fh.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  transmute(
    area_id,
    time_id,

  )

  left_join(fh_final_estimates, by = c("area_id", "time_id")) |>
  relocate(direct_estimate, n, .after = time_id)







However, the BHF and Fay–Herriot estimates for each small area can still differ because the two models use the survey information differently. The BHF model is fitted to unweighted respondent records, while the Fay–Herriot model starts from weighted direct estimates and their sampling variances to model area-year estimates. As a result, unstable direct estimates can affect the Fay–Herriot results, whereas the BHF model may be inaccurate if the complex survey design and weights are ignored. In general, for scenarios where rich survey microdata is present, a unit-level approach is preferred.
That said, although the model is fitted with unit-level predictors, the aggregation step relies on strong assumptions about each area’s population composition. Representing age, sex, and car access with area-level summaries, such as mean age, proportion female, and share of households with car access, can hide important compositional differences. Two areas may have similar summaries but very different age-sex-car structures, meaning the model could produce similar estimates even where walking behaviour differs across specific combinations of these predictors.
This limitation can be addressed by using a poststratification table that contains population counts for the joint distribution of the relevant predictors. This is the logic of Multilevel Regression with Poststratification (MRP), predict the outcome for each poststratification cell, then aggregate those predictions using the corresponding population counts so the final estimates better reflect the target population composition.


Code
write_csv(final_bhf_results, file.path(base_path, "freqwalk_estimates_bhf.csv"))

title: Small Area Estimation with Poststratification
text:
Theory in brief



Let c index poststratification cells within area j and time t. The cells are defined by whichever population variables are available for poststratification. In a unit-level MRP approach, a binary walking outcome can be modelled at the respondent level as

\begin{aligned}
Y_{ijt} &\sim \mathrm{Bernoulli}(\pi_{ijt}) \\
\mathrm{logit}(\pi_{ijt}) &=
\alpha + z_{ijt}^{T}\beta + u_j + v_t .
\end{aligned}

where z_{ijt} is a vector of respondent-level predictors used to define or adjust the poststratification cells, \beta contains their coefficients, u_j is an area effect, and v_t is a time effect. The fitted model gives predicted cell means for the binary frequent-walking indicator in each poststratification cell:

\hat{\pi}_{jtc}
=
\widehat{\mathbb{E}}(Y \mid j,t,c).

The poststratification step combines those cell predictions with population counts N_{jtc} available or estimated for the same cells. Area-time estimates are then population-weighted averages of the cell predictions. 
\hat{\mu}_{jt}^{\mathrm{MRP}}
=
\frac{\sum_c N_{jtc}\hat{\pi}_{jtc}}
{\sum_c N_{jtc}}.
Code
library(dplyr)
library(readr)
library(stringr)
library(tidyr)
library(sf)
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)
library(spdep)
library(INLA)
library(tibble)
library(purrr)
library(scales)

base_path <- here::here("data")
domain_frame <- read_csv(
  file.path(base_path, "clean", "domain_msoayear.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)
share_label <- label_percent(accuracy = 0.1)
pp_label <- label_number(accuracy = 0.1, scale = 100, suffix = " pp")

msoa_boundaries <- st_read(
  file.path(base_path, "boundaries-msoa.geojson"),
  quiet = TRUE
) |>
  rename(area_id = all_of("MSOA21CD")) |>
  filter(str_starts(area_id, "W"))

title: Small Area Estimation with Poststratification
text:
Estimation approach






Target estimand





Outcome and Population: Share of Adults who walk for transport daily
Geography: MSOAs in Wales
Time: 2021, 2023, and 2025




MRP extends the unit-level SAE workflow by combining a respondent-level outcome model with a poststratification table describing the target population. For our estimand, we model the binary frequent-walking indicator using age_band, sex, car_access, and spatial and temporal random effects. We then produce predicted cell means for the binary frequent-walking indicator for each age_band × sex × car_access population cell and aggregate them to MSOA-year estimates using population weights. Uncertainty is propagated by repeating this aggregation across posterior draws.
In the poststratification step, our poststratification tables with population counts for each age_band-sex-car_access cell for each MSOA were sourced from ONS UK Census 2021 so it only observes the composition for 2021. For the 2023 and 2025 estimands, the model can still estimate different area-time outcomes through the temporal and spatial terms, but the poststratification weights are held fixed, assuming that local demographic and car-access composition does not change across the survey years. In other words, N_{jtc} = N_{jc,2021} for all three waves.

title: Small Area Estimation with Poststratification
text:
2 Fit and evaluate models
Before fitting the model with INLA, as in previous methods, we first create consistent numeric indices for each MSOA and survey year, and a Queen-contiguity adjacency graph for the spatial effect for the modelling datasets.

area_levels <- sort(unique(domain_frame[["area_id"]]))
time_levels <- sort(unique(domain_frame[["time_id"]]))

area_index <- tibble(
  area_id = area_levels,
  area_inla_id = seq_along(area_levels)
)

time_index <- tibble(
  time_id = time_levels,
  time_inla_id = seq_along(time_levels)
)


msoa_boundaries_sorted <- msoa_boundaries |>
  inner_join(area_index, by = "area_id") |>
  arrange(area_inla_id)

msoa_neighbours <- poly2nb(
  msoa_boundaries_sorted,
  queen = TRUE,
  row.names = msoa_boundaries_sorted$area_id
)

spatial_graph_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".adj")

nb2INLA(
  file = spatial_graph_file,
  nb = msoa_neighbours
)


model_data <- model_data |>
  left_join(area_index, by = "area_id") |>
  left_join(time_index, by = "time_id") |>
  drop_na(indicator, age_band, sex, car_access, area_inla_id, time_inla_id)

poststrat_data <- poststrat_data |>
  left_join(area_index, by = "area_id") |>
  left_join(time_index, by = "time_id") |>
  drop_na(age_band, sex, car_access, area_inla_id, time_inla_id)

We fit a sequence of binomial unit-level models. The outcome is the respondent walking indicator, and fitted values for the poststratification rows are returned as response-scale cell means.



Model
Name
Specification




M0
Baseline
Temporal RW1 plus BYM2 spatial MSOA effect


M1
+Demographic
M0 plus age band and sex


M2
+CarAccess
M1 plus respondent car access




m0_formula <- indicator ~
  1 +
  f(time_inla_id, model = "rw1", constr = TRUE) +
  f(
    area_inla_id,
    model = "bym2",
    graph = spatial_graph_file,
    scale.model = TRUE,
    constr = TRUE
  )

m1_formula <- indicator ~
  age_band +
  sex +
  f(time_inla_id, model = "rw1", constr = TRUE) +
  f(
    area_inla_id,
    model = "bym2",
    graph = spatial_graph_file,
    scale.model = TRUE,
    constr = TRUE
  )

m2_formula <- indicator ~
  age_band +
  sex +
  car_access +
  f(time_inla_id, model = "rw1", constr = TRUE) +
  f(
    area_inla_id,
    model = "bym2",
    graph = spatial_graph_file,
    scale.model = TRUE,
    constr = TRUE
  )

model_formulas <- list(
  "M0 Baseline" = m0_formula,
  "M1 +Demographic" = m1_formula,
  "M2 +CarAccess" = m2_formula
)

The observed respondent rows and the poststratification rows are combined before fitting. Rows with indicator = NA are not used in the likelihood, but INLA still returns their fitted values, which are needed for poststratification.

model_poststrat_data <- bind_rows(
  model_data |>
    mutate(row_type = "model"),
  poststrat_data |>
    mutate(row_type = "poststrat", indicator = NA_real_
    )
) |>
  select(
    row_type, 
    indicator, 
    age_band, 
    sex,
    car_access,
    time_inla_id, 
    area_inla_id
    )

fit_mrp_model <- function(formula) {
  inla(
    formula = formula,
    family = "binomial",
    Ntrials = 1,
    data = model_poststrat_data,
    control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE, link = 1),
    control.compute = list(waic = TRUE, config = TRUE)
  )
}

mrp_fits <- lapply(model_formulas, fit_mrp_model)

As before, we use WAIC as an initial model check. The table ranks the candidate models by fit while keeping the response model aligned with the available poststratification cells.

title: Small Area Estimation with Poststratification
text:
3 Poststratification
At this point, having selected our final model, we use poststratification to convert its cell-level predictions into the target MSOA-year estimates. That means, each age_band x sex x car_access cell prediction is weighted by its population count, then aggregated within each MSOA-year. We can apply this calculation using the posterior mean cell values returned above, which gives a simple point estimate for each cell:


Code
poststrat_cell_rows <- which(model_poststrat_data$row_type == "poststrat")

cell_mean_predictions <- mrp_final_fit$summary.fitted.values |>
  as_tibble() |>
  slice(poststrat_cell_rows) |>
  transmute(cell_mean = mean)

cell_point_estimates <- bind_cols(poststrat_data, cell_mean_predictions)

area_year_point_estimates <- cell_point_estimates |>
  group_by(area_id, time_id) |>
  summarise(
    weighted_cell_sum = sum(cell_mean * pop_count),
    population_total = sum(pop_count),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(mrp_point_estimate = weighted_cell_sum / population_total) |>
  select(area_id, time_id, mrp_point_estimate)

However, the final output for SAE also needs uncertainty estimates. To propagate uncertainty through poststratification, we repeat the same population-weighted aggregation across posterior draws. The posterior draws used for this calculation are shown below.
The function inla.posterior.sample() gives plausible versions of the fitted model. For each draw, we keep the poststratification rows, convert fitted values from the logit scale to the original 0-1 scale, population-weight them within each MSOA-year, and summarise the resulting posterior distribution.

# Draw 300 posterior draws of the model fit
set.seed(100)
posterior_draws <- inla.posterior.sample(300, mrp_final_fit)

#  For each draw, keep the poststrat rows, convert values to the original scale 
predictor_rows <- startsWith(rownames(posterior_draws[[1]]$latent), "Predictor")
area_year_id <- paste(poststrat_data$area_id, poststrat_data$time_id, sep = "__")
poststrat_draws <- sapply(posterior_draws, \(draw) {
  plogis(as.numeric(draw$latent[predictor_rows, 1])[poststrat_cell_rows])
})

# Population-weight them
area_year_weighted_sums <- rowsum(poststrat_draws * poststrat_data$pop_count,
  group = area_year_id, reorder = FALSE)
area_year_populations <- rowsum(poststrat_data$pop_count,
  group = area_year_id, reorder = FALSE)
area_year_means <- area_year_weighted_sums / as.numeric(area_year_populations)

title: Small Area Estimation with Poststratification
text:
4 Final estimates and uncertainty
As with previous methods, we report the MRP estimates alongside the direct estimates and variance outputs in order to provide a full view of the direct survey evidence that accompanies the modelled estimates.


Code
direct_estimates <- read_csv(
  file.path(base_path, "freqwalk_estimates_direct.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
) |>
  select(area_id, time_id, n, direct_estimate, variance)

final_mrp_results <- final_mrp_results |>
  left_join(direct_estimates, by = c("area_id", "time_id")) |>
  mutate(
    direct_ci_width = 2 * qnorm(0.975) * sqrt(pmax(variance, 0))
  ) |>
  select(
    area_id,
    msoa_name,
    time_id,
    n,
    direct_estimate,
    variance,
    direct_ci_width,
    mrp_estimate,
    mrp_variance,
    mrp_lower,
    mrp_upper,
    mrp_ci_width
  )


The final estimates show frequent walking for transport increasing among Welsh adults across the three survey periods, with some higher-estimate clusters around urban areas. This pattern was difficult to see in the direct estimates because they were too unstable when aggregated to the desired MSOA level.










It is essential to caveat these estimates with the fact that we are reusing the same age-sex-car population composition of one year (2021) to estimate for the other two waves (2023, 2025) and letting the modelled time effect capture changes in the outcome. This is only possible if the relative age_band x sex x car_access poststratification weights stay consistent throughout the target periods, an assumption that must be made explicit.
Compared to estimates obtained from other modelling approaches, the MRP estimates are understandably very close to the BHF estimates. Agreement with the direct estimates is much weaker as expected, reflecting the instability of sparse MSOA-year survey cells. The Fay–Herriot estimates tend to sit lower than MRP for many cells, suggesting stronger shrinkage toward lower area-year rates.


Code
bhf_final_estimates <- read_csv(
  file.path(base_path, "freqwalk_estimates_bhf.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
) |>
  select(
    area_id,
    time_id,
    bhf_estimate,
    bhf_variance,
    bhf_ci_width
  )

fh_final_estimates <- read_csv(file.path(base_path, "freqwalk_estimates_fh.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  select(area_id, time_id, fh_estimate, fh_variance, fh_ci_width)

comparison_results <- final_mrp_results |>

title: Small Area Estimation with Poststratification
section: 5 Appendix: Enhance shallow poststratification with contextual predictors
text:
5 Appendix: Enhance shallow poststratification with contextual predictors
Sometimes the population table is available for every target year but only at a shallow cell grain. For example, ONS mid-year population estimates can give MSOA-year counts by age and sex, but not by car access. In that setting we can still use MRP, but the model may only specify two unit-level predictors represented in the poststratification table.
That said, contextual predictors can then be added to help explain between-area (or, between-year) variation. Since these predictors vary by MSOA, not by respondent within an MSOA, this is weaker than having unit-level predictors and matching poststratification cells because they cannot represent how walking behaviour differs between adults with and without car access inside the same age-sex cell.
Here is how the population poststratification data could look with only age_band and sex for three target years.


Code
shallow_poststrat_data <- read_csv(
  file.path(base_path, "clean", "poststrat_freqwalk_age_sex_212325.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
) |>
  filter(pop_count > 0) |>
  mutate(
    age_band = factor(age_band, levels = age_band_levels),
    sex = factor(sex, levels = c(1, 2), labels = c("Male", "Female"))
  ) |> 
  arrange(time_id, area_id, age_band, sex)

shallow_poststrat_summary <- shallow_poststrat_data |>
  group_by(time_id) |>
  summarise(
    poststrat_cells = n(),
    total_population = sum(pop_count),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

The contextual predictors can be added to both the model data and the poststratification data, as well as the coded area and time IDs for ingestion into INLA.


Code
area_context_predictors <- read_csv(
  file.path(base_path, "clean", "areapred_freqwalk.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
) |>
  transmute(
    area_id,
    population_density = scaled_population_density,
    car_access_hhshare = scaled_car_access_hhshare,
    share_students = scaled_share_students,
    share_work_from_home = scaled_share_work_from_home
  )

shallow_model_data <- shallow_model_data |>
  left_join(area_context_predictors, by = "area_id") |>
  left_join(area_index, by = "area_id") |>
  left_join(time_index, by = "time_id") |>
  drop_na(indicator, age_band, sex, population_density, car_access_hhshare,
          share_students, share_work_from_home, area_inla_id, time_inla_id)

shallow_poststrat_data <- shallow_poststrat_data |>
  left_join(area_context_predictors, by = "area_id") |>
  left_join(area_index, by = "area_id") |>
  left_join(time_index, by = "time_id") |>
  drop_na(age_band, sex, population_density, car_access_hhshare,
          share_students, share_work_from_home, area_inla_id, time_inla_id)


In the modelling step, the model specification uses age_band and sex as the poststratification-cell predictors, and adds the contextual area predictors directly as fixed effect terms.

shallow_context_formula <- indicator ~
  age_band +
  sex +
  population_density +
  car_access_hhshare +
  share_students +
  share_work_from_home +
  f(time_inla_id, model = "rw1", constr = TRUE) +
  f(
    area_inla_id,
    model = "bym2",
    graph = spatial_graph_file,
    scale.model = TRUE,
    constr = TRUE
  )

shallow_model_poststrat_data <- bind_rows(
  shallow_model_data |>
    mutate(row_type = "model"),
  shallow_poststrat_data |>
    mutate(row_type = "poststrat", indicator = NA_real_)
) |>
  select(
    row_type,
    indicator,
    age_band,
    sex,
    car_access_hhshare,
    population_density,
    share_work_from_home,
    share_students,
    time_inla_id,
    area_inla_id
  )

shallow_context_fit <- inla(
  formula = shallow_context_formula,
  family = "binomial",
  Ntrials = 1,
  data = shallow_model_poststrat_data,
  control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE, link = 1),
  control.compute = list(waic = TRUE, config = TRUE)
)

It is worth noting that a quick WAIC comparison with our earlier best-fitting age-sex-car model suggests that contextual predictors add less to model performance than being able to include the additional unit-level car-access predictor. Therefore, wherever survey microdata and poststratification data are available and compatible, we should opt for richer model specifications.


Code
rich_shallow_waic <- bind_rows(
  model_waic |>
    filter(model == mrp_bestmodel) |>
    transmute(
      workflow = "Rich MRP",
      model = "Age + Sex + CarAccess",
      waic,
      eff_params
    ),
  tibble(
    workflow = "Shallow MRP",
    model = "Age + Sex (+Contextual)",
    waic = shallow_context_fit$waic$waic,
    eff_params = shallow_context_fit$waic$p.eff
  )
) |>
  arrange(waic)

Finally, during the poststratification step, the fitted cell predictions are weighted only by the age-sex population counts for each MSOA-year to produce the estimates for each cell.


Code
shallow_poststrat_cell_rows <- which(shallow_model_poststrat_data$row_type == "poststrat")

set.seed(101)
shallow_posterior_draws <- inla.posterior.sample(300, shallow_context_fit)

shallow_predictor_rows <- startsWith(rownames(shallow_posterior_draws[[1]]$latent), "Predictor")
shallow_area_year_id <- paste(
  shallow_poststrat_data$area_id,
  shallow_poststrat_data$time_id,
  sep = "__"
)

shallow_poststrat_draws <- sapply(shallow_posterior_draws, \(draw) {
  plogis(as.numeric(draw$latent[shallow_predictor_rows, 1])[shallow_poststrat_cell_rows])
})

shallow_area_year_weighted_sums <- rowsum(
  shallow_poststrat_draws * shallow_poststrat_data$pop_count,
  group = shallow_area_year_id,
  reorder = FALSE
)
shallow_area_year_populations <- rowsum(
  shallow_poststrat_data$pop_count,
  group = shallow_area_year_id,
  reorder = FALSE
)
shallow_area_year_means <- shallow_area_year_weighted_sums / as.numeric(shallow_area_year_populations)

shallow_area_year_summary <- tibble(
  area_year_id = rownames(shallow_area_year_means),
  shallow_mrp_estimate = rowMeans(shallow_area_year_means),
  shallow_mrp_variance = apply(shallow_area_year_means, 1, var),
  shallow_mrp_lower = apply(shallow_area_year_means, 1, quantile, probs = 0.025, names = FALSE),
  shallow_mrp_upper = apply(shallow_area_year_means, 1, quantile, probs = 0.975, names = FALSE)
) |>
  mutate(shallow_mrp_ci_width = shallow_mrp_upper - shallow_mrp_lower) |>
  separate(area_year_id, into = c("area_id", "time_id"), sep = "__", convert = TRUE)

shallow_mrp_results <- domain_frame |>
  select(area_id, msoa_name, time_id) |>
  left_join(shallow_area_year_summary, by = c("area_id", "time_id"))

Compared with the richer three-predictor MRP model, the local differences show whether estimates are driven more by detailed population composition or broader area context. The shallow model may raise estimates in areas where contextual predictors suggest favourable walking conditions (e.g., high population density), while the rich model may lower them if the poststratification cells contain more residents with car access than the area-level car-ownership contextual predictor implies.
